Billings neighborhoods and why they matter

Billings lies in the Yellowstone Valley at 3,126 feet, and sandstone cliffs known as the Rims (or Rimrocks) run through town. They curve north and east of downtown, which is what separates it from the Heights and from Lockwood. The city's 2025 population estimate is 121,239.

  • Downtown and the valley floor: older homes near the Yellowstone River.
  • Billings Heights: north of the Rims along U.S. Highway 87, which becomes Main Street inside the city.
  • Lockwood: east of downtown.
  • South Hills, West End and Shiloh: reached from Interstate 90 and Montana Highway 3.

Views of the Rims and easy access to the trails along the cliffs deserve a line in any listing. Healthcare is the biggest source of jobs, with Billings Clinic at about 4,500 workers and St. Vincent Regional Hospital at about 2,200, which keeps hospital staff in the pool of local buyers.

Hail, snow and older roofs

Billings summers are hot and dry, winters cold and dry. An average year brings 57.4 inches of snow, though chinook winds melt much of it fast. Hail is what drives roof inspections. On June 20, 2010, a tornado brought hail up to golf ball size through the Heights and downtown.

Old shingles tend to show up in an inspector's report, and a repair request can delay a closing that depends on a mortgage. Many owners with tired roofs sell as is instead, which avoids the back and forth and lets the offer account for the work.

Property tax in Billings and Yellowstone County

Yellowstone County's treasurer sends Billings tax bills and sits at 2825 3rd Avenue North, Room 113 (406-256-2802). Dates track the state calendar apart from a one-time shift in this cycle.

Real estate paymentYellowstone County date
First halfNovember 30 (2026 only: December 3)
Second halfMay 31 (2027 only: June 1)
Deadline time5 p.m. Mountain Time, next business day if a weekend or holiday
Late payment2% penalty and 5/6 of 1% interest per month

Under the 2026 state rates, a lived-in home or long-term rental starts at 0.76% on the first $378,000 and climbs by tier. Second homes, short-term rentals and vacant lots are charged a flat 1.90%.

If the valuation looks wrong, the notice date starts a 30-day clock. Use it to file Form AB-26 with the Department of Revenue or to appeal at the county tax appeal board directly.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Billings house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Listing, owner sale or cash

Billings owners usually compare three paths. Each gives up something different.

  • Agent listing: the widest audience, paid for with a commission, open houses and whatever repairs the inspection requests.
  • Owner sale: you keep the commission and take on the advertising, the contract and the forms.
  • Cash offer: one buyer, usually taking the house as is, with a closing date set around you.

All three finish at the courthouse. A notary acknowledges the deed, and the county clerk and recorder files it together with a Realty Transfer Certificate. Recording costs $20 for page one and $10 for every added page. Tax you still owe on the house sits as a lien, and the closing clears it.

To get a cash offer on your Billings house, describe it in the form above. You will receive an offer in writing, and saying no costs nothing.

How a cash sale unfolds

The process starts with the form on this page: address, a few details about the house. After we review the property and title, a written offer follows. Read it at your own pace; countering or declining is fine and carries no fee. Once you agree, a title company opens a file, verifies ownership and finds every lien, unpaid property tax included. A closing date is set to suit you, the deed and certificate go to the county clerk and recorder, and your money is released after any loan or tax payoff.

There is no repair list, no parade of showings and no underwriter to wait on. The trade-off is less competition among buyers than a listing creates, which is exactly why a side-by-side written comparison pays off.

If you owe tax on the house

An open balance with Yellowstone County is not a dealbreaker. Late bills pick up a 2% penalty plus 5/6 of 1% interest per month, so the total keeps rising until it is settled. Get today's balance from the treasurer's office, pass it to the title company, and the payment comes out of what you receive at closing. When a lender handles tax through escrow, confirm that first so nothing is paid twice.

The same step applies to any other lien on the title. Whoever you sell to, ask for a settlement statement ahead of closing day and check each line against your own records, including the tax line and the recording fee.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Billings houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What goes in the closing file

A deed, a Realty Transfer Certificate and the recording fee make up the package that goes to the county clerk and recorder. Sale prices on the certificate feed the Department of Revenue's mass appraisal of Montana real property, so the number you report can affect how neighbors' homes are valued later.

  • Seller and buyer names should match across the certificate and the deed.
  • Each party supplies the last four digits of a Social Security or employer identification number.
  • No recording happens until a notary has acknowledged the deed.

From the moment it is filed, a recorded deed counts as notice to any later buyer or lender.

Before you decide, a short checklist

Pull out your newest tax statement first and check whether the first half is paid. When the amount or date is murky, phone the county treasurer, because this cycle's dates slide by a few days. Then inspect the roof, since hail comes up more than anything else. After that, choose between the reach of a listing and the quickness of a cash sale. A known lien should go to the title company on day one so a payoff number waits for you at signing.

Selling for cash as is removes the lender's appraisal, repair demands and loan approval delay. The offer is priced to the house's condition, so line it up against your likely net from a listing once commission, repairs and holding costs come off. Also ask who covers recording costs and the date your money arrives.

Mention it if the house was a rental of either kind. Its tax class shapes next year's bill for the buyer, and someone moving in can apply for the lower scale.

Frequently asked questions

When are Yellowstone County property taxes due?

The first half of real estate tax is due November 30, with December 3 as the 2026 date, and the second half is due May 31, with June 1 in 2027. Payments are due by 5 p.m. Mountain Time.

What rate applies to a Billings primary residence in 2026?

A tiered rate that begins at 0.76% on the first $378,000 of value. Second homes, short-term rentals and vacant lots pay a flat 1.90%.

Does Billings get hail?

Yes. A June 20, 2010 tornado came with hail up to golf ball size and damaged downtown, the Heights and the MetraPark Arena. Roof condition is a common point in a Billings sale.

Can I sell my Billings house as is?

Yes. A cash buyer can purchase a Billings house in its present condition, and the sale still requires a recorded deed and a Realty Transfer Certificate.

What does it cost to record a deed in Billings?

The standard fee is $20 for the first page and $10 for each added page, paid to the county clerk and recorder when the deed and certificate are filed.

Missoula context for sellers

Missoula is the seat of Missoula County in western Montana, spread along the Clark Fork River where the Bitterroot and Blackfoot rivers meet it. Five mountain ranges converge here, which earned it the nickname hub of five valleys. Elevation is 3,209 feet.

Two peaks, Sentinel and Jumbo, crowd the edge of town, and plenty of streets dead-end at a hillside. Hillside lots raise drainage, access and foundation questions a valley-floor lot never does, and buyers bring them up early. Homes near the university and old downtown tend to be older, on tighter lots. North Reserve Street, where Highway 93 crosses the old Mullan Road with quick access to Interstate 90, has been the main retail district since the late 1990s.

The University of Montana, Missoula County Public Schools, St. Patrick Hospital and Community Medical Center drive local housing demand. Staff, students and renters keep looking for places near campus and the hospitals, and moves in and out of town are common.

Snow, heat and your roof

Winters are cold and moderately snowy, summers hot and dry. Snow averages 39.5 inches a season, usually falling between October 30 and April 20, and snow cover lasts roughly four months.

An inspector's eye goes straight to the roof. Sagging decking, weak attic ventilation and ice dams all show up fast. The furnace gets scrutiny too: December averages 23.9 degrees, and January 1957 hit minus 33 degrees.

Summer cuts the other way, with about 24 days a year at 90 degrees or higher and a peak of 107 degrees, last reached June 30, 2021. Many older neighborhoods have no air conditioning, and buyers feel it during a July showing.

Rivers matter as well. Near the Clark Fork or the Bitterroot? Look at the county floodplain maps first.

Due dates and penalties

Real property tax in Missoula County is split into a November payment and a May payment, each due by the month's final day. If that day is a weekend or holiday, you get the next business day, except for people who received help from the state revenue department's assistance program.

One invoice covers both halves and arrives in late October or early November, so do not wait for a second bill in the spring. The Treasurer's Office takes payment in person, online or by mail, and mailed checks must be postmarked by the deadline.

StageConsequence
After the due date2% penalty plus interest at a 10% annual rate
Late June or early JulyDelinquent notices go out
First business day of AugustTax lien attaches; $75 lien certificate fee
Late AugustOutside investors may buy the lien

From the day a lien attaches, the owner gets two to three years to pay up before the house itself is in danger.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Missoula house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Selling with taxes owed

A tax bill you have not paid will not stop a sale, but it must be settled by the time of closing. Have the title company get a payoff figure, then check it against the county's online lookup. If the two differ, phone the Treasurer's Office before closing day. The balance is subtracted from your proceeds.

Sorting this out before you list keeps closing day calm. Any buyer's title commitment will surface tax items and liens, and they are easier to clear while no clock is running.

How to dispute your property valuation

Your home's value comes from the state rather than the county. Residential property is reappraised on a two-year cycle, and the time to object is when the notice shows up.

Two paths exist. The first is Form AB-26, a Request for Informal Classification and Appraisal Review that goes to the department. The second is a direct appeal to the Missoula County Tax Appeal Board. File either one on the state's tax appeal website. Timing is set by state law: object within 30 days of the date on the notice and the result covers both years of the cycle; object later and it covers only the second year, with June 1 as the limit.

Selling while an appeal is open? Your closing figure stays at the billed amount until a decision comes. Pay what is billed and the title company will prorate it. A lower value may cut a later bill.

Your property record card is public, with building, land and characteristic details posted online. Scan it for wrong square footage or bedroom counts before anything else.

Building permits and work without them

Inside city limits, new one and two unit dwellings need a permit and must follow the International Residential Code. Small projects can be exempt. A free-standing residential deck 30 inches or less above the ground is one example.

Unpermitted work is where sellers get stuck. Inspectors and lenders may want permit records for a finished basement, an addition or a garage conversion. Development Services has a page section devoted to work done without a permit. The Zoning Desk takes email, or calls between 10 am and 2 pm at (406) 552-6625.

Property outside the city falls under Missoula County, which has its own guide at missoulacounty.build. Before any repair, find out which office covers your address.

  • Find the parcel on the county property information system.
  • Ask whether past additions were permitted.
Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Missoula houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Transit and airport

Mountain Line runs 14 bus routes serving Missoula, East Missoula, Bonner, Target Range, Rattlesnake and the airport, with paratransit and four park and ride lots. Missoula Montana Airport, run by the Missoula County Airport Authority, is the largest in western Montana. Passenger rail ended in 1979 when Amtrak dropped the North Coast Hiawatha.

What Missoula sellers usually run into

  • Roofs and attics worn by decades of snow load.
  • Older homes near campus with deferred maintenance.
  • Inherited houses that need a probate step before they can transfer.
  • Tax bills split across several districts, including city, county, fire and water.
  • Slope, drainage or floodplain questions that surface late in escrow.

Paying cash can shorten that list since no lender appraisal stands in the way, though price and terms still track the house's condition. Weigh any offer against what a listing would net you.

Order a title commitment early, whatever the sale route, so liens and tax items are known. The Clerk and Recorder keeps deeds, surveys and land books searchable online, which helps you confirm the legal description and any easements on your lot.

What to gather before you list

A thin folder now saves time later. Put in your latest tax invoice, your lender's payoff figure, permit records for any addition or finished basement, and notes on the roof and heating. Inherited house? Ask about probate first, because the deed cannot move until it is done. A quick search of the county's deed and record pages confirms your legal description before a title company asks.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

When are property taxes due in Missoula County?

Each half is due by the end of November and the end of May. If the date is a weekend or holiday, the next business day applies. One bill covers both halves.

What is the penalty for late property tax in Missoula?

Expect a 2% penalty and 10% annual interest. The lien attaches the first business day of August, after which the owner has two to three years to pay.

Who sets my home's value in Missoula?

The state does, on a two-year reappraisal cycle. Disagree? File Form AB-26 for an informal review, or go straight to the county's tax appeal board.

Does a Missoula house need a permit for a deck?

Sometimes not. A free-standing residential deck at 30 inches or less above grade can be exempt, along with other criteria. Attached or taller decks call for a conversation with Development Services.

Can I sell a Missoula house with an unpaid tax bill?

Yes. Closing takes the balance out of your proceeds after the title company gets a payoff figure. Settling it before listing means fewer surprises.

Great Falls and Malmstrom

Great Falls, in central Montana, is the Cascade County seat and ranks third in size among the state's cities: 60,442 people in 22.9 square miles at the 2020 count, inside a county of 84,414. The Missouri River flows through, and dams on three of its falls produce the hydropower behind the Electric City nickname.

No employer matters more to local housing than Malmstrom Air Force Base. The base counts about 3,371 active-duty members, 525 Air Force civilians and some 3,300 family members on or near the property, and put its fiscal year 2025 economic impact near $444 million.

Assignments rotate on a schedule, and a family holding orders may have only a short window to leave. Waiting on a buyer's loan approval can feel painfully slow in that position.

  • With orders in hand, give your report date to every buyer and agent at the outset.
  • Compare how long a cash closing takes against a financed one.
  • Say whether the house is vacant, which can move the closing date.

Freeze, thaw and what weather does to a house

Long, snowy winters, hot dry summers and the occasional chinook wind define the year here, and winter afternoons top 50 degrees about fifteen times over three months. Expect big swings: 20.8 nights at 0 degrees or colder, 44 days that never get above freezing, and about nineteen days reaching 90 degrees.

Freeze and thaw cycles punish foundations and driveways. Roofs deal with snow and summer storms, and furnaces and water heaters work through long heating seasons. Put an aging roof or a shaky furnace in your disclosure, since a buyer's inspector will find it anyway.

Who to call in Great Falls

QuestionOffice and phone

Code enforcement

Complaints drive property code enforcement in Great Falls, and the usual subjects are rubbish, junk vehicles and upkeep. A neighbor's complaint can leave an open case that complicates a sale, so close it out before listing or tell the buyer what is outstanding. Nine neighborhood councils give you a way to hear what is going on near your street.

To clear an open case, start with the right office: Planning and Community Development for anything on private property, Public Works for the public right-of-way. Ask what has to be fixed, fix it, and keep a note of the date and who confirmed it. A buyer or title company that asks about the property will then get a straight answer, and a cash buyer will not need to discount the offer for an unknown.

How Great Falls property taxes are billed

The county mails residential bills in late October and collects the money. One half is due November 30, or 30 days after the postmark if that is later, and the other half May 31. Homes are revalued every two years at 100 percent of market value. The property tax office is at 121 4th Street North, Suite 1A.

The title company usually settles any unpaid tax for the current period at closing. Request a payoff figure beforehand so the amount is no surprise at signing.

What a seller must tell the buyer

Montana expects a Great Falls seller to disclose in writing any adverse material facts the seller really knows. Section 70-20-502 names title issues, water and wastewater systems, structural and mechanical trouble, additions built without a permit, hazardous materials, drainage and soil problems, and radon, mold or lead-based paint testing.

Deliver it before or alongside the contract; if it arrives later, section 70-20-504 lets the buyer rescind within three days. Section 70-20-503 lists lighter duties for court-ordered transfers, foreclosure sales, transfers to a spouse, child or parent, and transfers between co-owners.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Great Falls houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Steps for a seller with orders

If a transfer set your move date, work backward from it. Confirm the amount you owe on any mortgage and on property tax. Decide if you can afford to wait on a financed buyer, or whether you need a date you control. The title company will want your latest tax statement, your mortgage payoff and the names on the deed. An empty house is worth mentioning to buyers. Once the deed is recorded your proceeds arrive, and you can leave on your report date with the house done.

Cash sidesteps the lender's appraisal and underwriting, the two steps likeliest to push a closing back. The trade is price, since the offer accounts for repairs and risk, so compare written numbers before you decide.

Listing, selling yourself or cash

Three routes are realistic. Pick based on the house's condition and your deadline.

  • Traditional listing. Most buyers see it, though showings, an inspection and a buyer's loan add time and may bring repair requests.
  • For sale by owner. The agent's commission stays with you, along with the marketing, the negotiating and the disclosure forms.
  • Cash sale to a house-buying company. The buyer accepts the property as is, no loan needs approval, and closing can be timed around your move. The price covers the repairs and risk the buyer absorbs, so measure the written offer against your likely net from a listing.

No cash offer is guaranteed. A buyer has to see the house and the title first.

A walkthrough before you list

Tour the house with an inspector's eye. Examine the foundation and driveway for freeze and thaw damage, the roof after a summer storm, and the furnace and water heater before the heating season starts. Clear rubbish, junk vehicles and overgrowth so a code complaint cannot surface mid-sale. Next, list what you know: repairs you made, problems you noticed and any addition built without a permit. That list becomes your disclosure, and handing it over early avoids the three-day rescission problem.

Finally, gather your tax paperwork. The county property tax office at 406-454-6850 can say what has been paid, and the title company uses that figure at closing.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Situations that push owners to sell

  • A military move tied to a report date.
  • An older house by the river or downtown with tired wiring, plumbing or roofing.
  • An inherited house shared by several heirs, some out of state.
  • An open code complaint over junk, rubbish or an unmaintained yard.
  • A rental, either with tenants or with deferred repairs, that the owner is tired of managing.

Frequently asked questions

How fast can I sell a house in Great Falls?

Timing depends on the title, the buyer and how ready you are. A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and loan approval, which are the steps that often slow a financed sale.

Do I need to fix a Great Falls house before selling it for cash?

No. A cash buyer purchases the house as it is. You still must disclose problems you know about under Montana law.

Who do I call about a code complaint on my Great Falls property?

For private property, call Planning and Community Development at 406-455-8574. For the public right-of-way, call Public Works at 406-771-1401.

When are Cascade County property taxes due?

The first half is due November 30, or within 30 days of the postmark if that is later, and the second half is due May 31. The county property tax office can be reached at 406-454-6850.

Is the Malmstrom workforce a reason Great Falls homes sell quickly?

Malmstrom is the largest employer in the community, and the base reports about 3,300 family members on or near it. How quickly any one house sells still depends on its condition, location and price.

Bozeman at a glance

Bozeman lies in the Gallatin Valley of southwest Montana, 4,817 feet above sea level. Butte is 84 miles away to the west, Billings 125 miles to the east, and Yellowstone National Park 93 miles south. Interstate 90 passes through. The count in 2020 was 53,293 people, the 2025 estimate is 58,814, and the wider metro area holds about 118,960.

Bozeman Health and Montana State University head the employer list, with firms such as Simms Fishing Products and Mystery Ranch behind them and a growing group of technology and biotech companies. Jobs like these keep newcomers arriving, so a Bozeman house usually draws interest. The questions sellers ask tend to be about tax rates and paperwork rather than demand.

Snow, ice and an older house

Long, snowy winters and fairly warm summers shape Bozeman houses, and the air at 4,817 feet can cool sharply after sundown. Up to 24 inches of precipitation falls in a year. Inspectors tend to study how the roof handles snow load, whether ice builds at the eaves and how the exterior wood has held up.

Deferred repairs do not have to be finished before a sale. Cash buyers accept the house as is and price in the work that remains, while a buyer with a mortgage may come back with a repair list after inspection.

Gallatin County's treasurer takes Bozeman payments at 311 West Main, Room 103. Call 406-582-3030 or write treasurer@gallatin.mt.gov between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday to Friday. Value disputes and taxable value questions belong to the Department of Revenue's Bozeman office, 406-582-3400.

  • Let the title company know who pays the county tax, you or a lender.
  • Make sure names match exactly on the deed and the Realty Transfer Certificate.
  • Sign the deed before a notary.
  • Check that the clerk and recorder gets the deed, certificate and fee.
  • Read the settlement statement before funds go out.
  • Keep a copy of the recorded deed and the final statement for your tax records.

Nothing here is hard, but each step depends on another person, so beginning a week early takes out most of the stress. Should a lien or unpaid tax surface, the title company takes it from your proceeds and closing carries on.

Calling or visiting the treasurer

Have your address or parcel number, your latest statement and the name on the account in front of you. Then ask three things: which halves are already paid, whether December 7, 2026 applies to your parcel, and what the payoff would be on a specific closing date. A call before you accept an offer prevents a hiccup at the signing table. A question about why the value is what it is goes to the Department of Revenue's Bozeman office instead.

A rough timeline for a cash sale

The first stage is the offer. You describe the house, we answer in writing, and you choose. Acceptance sends the file to a title company, which searches the record for liens and unpaid tax and drafts the documents. After the notary signing, the deed and certificate are recorded and money moves once the settlement statement is approved. With a mortgage buyer, an appraisal and lender review sit in the middle, and that is usually where schedules stretch.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Tax owed at sale

Pay late and you owe a 2% penalty plus 5/6 of 1% interest each month, while the unpaid amount turns into a lien on the house. Selling is still an option. The treasurer's office gives you the balance, the title company receives it, and the amount comes out of your proceeds when you close. With cash there is no lender approval to hold things up. The treasurer answers payment questions, and the Department of Revenue's Bozeman office explains the value behind your bill.

Bozeman also has a Community Housing Program run by the city, which publishes housing data and help resources for people who live, work and study in town. It is worth a look if you are weighing a sale against staying.

Frequently asked questions

Who collects property tax in Bozeman?

The Gallatin County Treasurer, at 311 West Main, Room 103. The Department of Revenue's Bozeman office handles questions about market and taxable value.

What is the 2026 property tax rate on a Bozeman primary residence?

A tiered rate: 0.76% on the first $378,000 of market value, 0.90% from $378,001 to $756,000, 1.10% from $756,001 to $1,511,999 and 1.90% above that. Second homes and short-term rentals pay a flat 1.90%.

When is the 2026 first-half tax payment due in Bozeman?

December 7, 2026 for the first half of 2026 real property tax, as Gallatin County lists it. State default dates are November 30 and May 31, each at 5 p.m.

Which school districts cover Bozeman?

Almost all of Bozeman is in the Bozeman Elementary and Bozeman High School Districts. A small area is in the Belgrade districts.

Can I sell my Bozeman house as is?

Yes. The sale still needs a notarized deed, a Realty Transfer Certificate and recording with the county clerk and recorder.

Selling in Butte?

Butte and Butte-Silver Bow

Silver Bow County and the city of Butte merged into one government, Butte-Silver Bow, which spreads over about 718 square miles. The dense core is a small piece of that, so a Butte address can mean a steep Uptown street or open ground well out of town. The 2020 census counted 34,494 residents.

Butte straddles the Continental Divide, where I-15 meets I-90. Plenty of houses date from the copper boom, and mining headframes still stand among the neighborhoods, so buyers ask what has been updated. Work comes from energy companies such as NorthWestern Energy, healthcare and Montana Technological University.

Butte Superfund cleanup and your house

Your yard may be tested for lead, and the testing area just grew. On September 21, 2026, the EPA finalized a Record of Decision Amendment for the Butte Priority Soils Operable Unit. It lowers the residential soil-lead cleanup level from 1,200 parts per million to 456 ppm and expands the Residential Metals Abatement Program area by about 3,627 acres. Over 7,000 more properties now qualify for assessment and, if needed, cleanup.

Under the selected remedy, a property is divided into decision units such as the front yard, back yard, play area and driveway. Each unit is sampled, and any unit above 456 ppm is excavated and replaced with clean fill. Properties sampled earlier that passed under the old 1,200 ppm level will be reevaluated. EPA expects sampling and cleanup in the expanded area to take roughly 15 years from 2026.

For a seller that comes down to four things:

  • Buyers may want to know if your lot was sampled and how it came out.
  • A yard that passed before may be looked at again under the lower level.
  • The program does the cleanup itself, so find out what applies to your address before listing.
  • Montana law requires you to disclose known adverse material facts, which includes any testing or treatment for lead-based paint or contaminated soil that you know about.

Butte cash buyers already know the program, which means they price the question in instead of finding it during an inspection.

Historic rules for old Uptown buildings

The Butte-Silver Bow Historic Preservation Commission reviews demolition permits for historic properties anywhere in the county except Walkerville. Its role also includes design review for properties on the Local Register and for properties that receive local funds or tax credits.

Selling does not start a review. A buyer's plans can. When an Uptown building in poor shape is headed for demolition or alteration, the permit counter becomes part of the story. Owners of Local Register houses or houses inside a historic district should say so at the first conversation, before the deal drifts.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Butte house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Property tax in Butte-Silver Bow

Butte-Silver Bow sends one real estate bill a year and collects it in halves: on or before November 30, then on or before May 31 of the next year. If your notice was postmarked late, the first half is not due until 30 days after the postmark. A Saturday, Sunday or holiday deadline slides to the next business day.

Homes are revalued every two years at 100 percent of market value, and the graduated state rate for homes applies without any application from the owner. For your own current figure, call the county treasurer.

Years of unpaid tax can end in a county tax deed sale. Short of that, a balance is normally paid from your proceeds at closing, and an early payoff request to the title company shows you the amount.

Disclosure duties in Montana

Sellers owe the buyer a written statement of adverse material facts they actually know about. The statute is section 70-20-502 of the Montana Code, and the statement must come before the contract or with it. Topics include title, water and wastewater, utility hookups, structural and mechanical systems, work done without a building permit, hazardous materials, soil and drainage, and any testing for asbestos, radon, lead-based paint, mold or contaminated soil.

Late delivery gives the buyer three days to cancel in writing under section 70-20-504, unless the offer already waived that right. Section 70-20-503 exempts certain transfers: court-ordered ones like probate, foreclosure sales, gifts to a spouse, child or parent, moves between co-owners, and sales where the contract waives the statement.

Choosing how to sell

Three paths are open: an agent, a sale by owner, or cash. Which one fits depends on the house's condition and how fast you must close.

  • Agent. Reaches the most buyers, at the price of showings, inspection requests and a lender. Older systems may need work first.
  • By owner. No listing commission, but marketing, forms and the disclosure statement are yours alone.
  • Cash. The buyer takes the house as it stands, with no lender appraisal and a closing date you can negotiate. Because the offer prices in condition and the buyer's costs, line it up in writing against your net from a listing.

On any route, work out the net after taxes, liens, loan payoff and closing costs. That figure is what lands in your account.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Butte houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling an inherited or neglected house

Many Butte sales start with a house nobody lives in. If several heirs share it, agree on who has authority to sign before you take an offer, because a buyer and title company will want to see that settled. If the estate has not closed, the person with legal authority over it signs, and a court-ordered transfer is exempt from the disclosure statement. Back taxes on a vacant building come out of the proceeds at closing, so ask for the payoff early.

For any older Butte house, a short folder of facts helps a buyer decide quickly: what has been updated, whether the yard was ever sampled for lead, any work done without a permit, and the latest tax statement. A cash buyer can work from that folder and give you a written offer without a lender's review.

Situations Butte sellers run into

SituationWhat usually helps
Inherited house with several heirs and an open estateSettle who can sign before taking offers
Older Uptown property where a financed buyer asks for repairsConsider a cash sale as is
Vacant or neglected building with back taxesRequest a payoff and clear it at closing
Uncertainty about soil testing under the Superfund programAsk the program about your address and disclose what you know
Tenants in place on a rental you want to be rid ofDisclose the tenancy at the start

Frequently asked questions

Do I have to fix my Butte house before I sell?

No. Montana law requires you to disclose known adverse material facts, not to repair them. A cash buyer purchases as is, and a listing buyer may ask for repairs after an inspection.

Will the Butte Superfund lead cleanup stop me from selling?

No rule in the September 2026 amendment bars a sale. It lowers the cleanup level to 456 ppm and expands the testing area, so a buyer may ask whether your property has been sampled. Contact the program about your address and disclose anything you know.

When are Butte-Silver Bow property taxes due?

Real estate taxes are due on or before November 30 and May 31. Check your notice, because the first payment can be due 30 days after the postmark if that is later.

What happens to unpaid property tax when I sell?

The title company normally pays the balance from your proceeds at closing. Ask for a payoff figure early so there are no surprises.

Is a seller disclosure statement required for an inherited house?

Transfers ordered by a probate court are exempt under section 70-20-503, and so are transfers to a spouse, child or parent of the owner. Other sales from an estate may still need the statement, so confirm with a title company or attorney.

Helena in brief

The state capital is also the Lewis and Clark County seat. At the 2020 count it had 32,091 people in about 17 square miles, and 83,058 lived in the metro area spanning Lewis and Clark and Jefferson counties. Helena fills part of the Helena Valley, Tenmile Creek crosses it, and hillside neighborhoods climb the edges. On a hillside lot a buyer weighs the slope, the access road and fire exposure.

Public employers carry the local economy: about 18 percent of working Helenans hold state agency jobs, and county, federal, school and medical employers fill out the rest. Many buyers come from those fields. Sellers who relocate, retire or inherit tend to want a closing date they can count on. Parts of town have Victorian homes from the gold camp years, which some buyers love and others fear.

Climate and your roof

Little rain or snow reaches Helena, just 11.4 inches a year, most of it in spring, yet winters are long and cold and summers hot. Recorded temperatures run from 105 degrees Fahrenheit down to minus 42. Roof, siding and foundation all get a hard look from inspectors because of that range.

Zoning, hillsides and accessory units

The city's zoning code says its regulations seek to minimize danger from wildland fires, stormwater flooding, soil erosion and other environmental hazards, to mitigate traffic hazards and to protect the scenic character of hillside areas. Chapter 2 of Title 11 of the Helena City Code sets out the land uses allowed in each district.

The same chapter covers accessory dwelling units. Only a single-dwelling unit residence may have one, and only one per lot, with a detached or attached ADU capped at 75 percent of the main house or 1,000 square feet, whichever comes first. A garage apartment or converted basement should be checked with the city for a permit and for fit within those limits, since an unpermitted unit must be disclosed.

A simple checklist for a sale:

  • Look up your lot's zoning district on the city planning pages.
  • Find permits for additions, finished basements and any second unit.
  • Note any hillside, drainage or access issues you know of.
  • Collect records for roof, furnace and chimney work.

How and when Helena property tax is paid

Roughly 37,000 real estate tax bills a year go out from Lewis and Clark County. They are mailed by the treasurer in late October, with the first payment due November 30 (or within 30 days of the postmark, whichever comes later) and the second due May 31.

Helena sellers owe buyers a written list of known adverse material facts. Hillside and wildfire questions buyers ask

Because the zoning code names wildland fire and hillside character as concerns, buyers of homes on slopes often ask about access for fire crews, drainage and erosion, and how well the lot is cleared. Have answers ready. Clear dry brush and woodpiles, note any retaining walls or drainage work you have done, and keep your roof and chimney records together. Ask your insurer for a written statement of current coverage, because a buyer may want to see it. None of this requires spending money before a sale, but a seller who has the facts ready tends to hold buyers' interest, while a buyer who has to guess usually lowers the price.

Selling a house you inherited

Helena has many long-time government and school families, so inherited houses come up often. Settle who has legal authority over the estate before you take offers, since that person signs. Court-ordered probate transfers skip the seller disclosure statement, though other estate sales may not, and the title company or an attorney can tell you which case yours is.

Gather the newest tax statement, permit records, notes on the roof, furnace and chimney, and the history of any second unit. When heirs are scattered, settle the lowest acceptable price and the closing date early so no single person stalls the deal. A cash buyer takes the house as is, which suits owners who cannot supervise repairs from far away.

Use the form here to describe the house and a written offer follows. Accepting it sends the file to a title company, which verifies ownership, finds liens and drafts the papers. The closing date can fit your plans. When you close, your mortgage and any unpaid tax go first and you keep the rest. Cash as is skips the lender's appraisal and the repair requests that tend to follow an inspection. Because condition shapes the price, set the written offer beside what a listing would net once commission and repairs are paid.

Montana's disclosure statement asks about additions made without a building permit. Contact the city's Building Division to check what is on file.

How many accessory dwelling units can I have on a Helena lot?

One. The city code allows one ADU per lot, accessory to a single-dwelling unit residence, and limits it to 75 percent of the main house or 1,000 square feet, whichever is less.

Kalispell housing context

Flathead County's seat and northwest Montana's biggest city, Kalispell counted 24,558 people in 2020. The elevation is 3,084 feet, with Flathead Lake roughly 7 miles south. Hospital work is the largest source of jobs, anchored by Logan Health Medical Center, and the ski and visitor trade around Whitefish Mountain Resort brings seasonal jobs. Expect buyers who live here year-round and others shopping for a second home.

Winter arrives around late October and lingers through March, cold and moderately snowy. Summer is hot and dry. Your roof holds snow for about five months and your furnace works hard, so buyers ask how old each one is. Look up the install dates before you list. Because summers run dry, a tidy yard and a well-kept exterior help at showings.

Due dates and late dates

Taxes in Flathead County come in two installments, and the Treasurer handles billing and collection. Stop by at 290 A North Main in Kalispell or call 406-758-5680.

PaymentDue dateDelinquent after
First halfNovember 30December 1
Second halfMay 31June 1

When the date lands on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, you have until 5:00 p.m. on the next business day. The first bill is mailed no later than 30 days before November 30. If it goes out late, your 30 days run from the postmark.

Monthly payment plan for a primary residence

Section 15-16-122 of the Montana Code gives primary-residence owners a way to spread the year's tax over seven monthly payments between November 30 and May 31. File by September 30 of the taxing year. A request made after that misses the cutoff for that year.

A seller can use the plan to keep the account in good standing during a listing. Whatever remains unpaid at the closing table is taken from your proceeds.

How Montana values your home and sets the rate

Valuation happens every two years, and the state counts 100 percent of market value. For tax year 2025, a home's rate climbs in steps: 0.76 percent applies to the first $400,000, then 1.10 percent to the slice up to $1.5 million, then 2.20 percent past that. Local levies are added, so the final bill turns on where your value falls.

Buyers like to search the online tax lookup for houses they tour. Run the search on your own address first so nothing surprises you.

Short-term rental and accessory unit rules

Where the house sits decides which rulebook applies, and that matters most for a former vacation rental. Inside Kalispell, the municipal code carries short-term residential rental standards and accessory dwelling unit provisions. Outside it, Flathead County writes its own regulations.

The county treats a dwelling built for stays under 30 days as a short-term rental. Across most zoned areas, an administrative conditional use permit is the requirement. Expect a review lasting up to a month and a half, with notice mailed to every owner within 150 feet. A few zones permit the use outright, others forbid it, and land with no zoning needs nothing from Planning and Zoning.

Whoever buys, with cash or a mortgage, will ask if the permit is current and whether it carries over. Phone the planning office first, then file the permit papers with your sale documents.

What you must tell a buyer in Montana

Montana expects a written statement of known defects from the seller. It addresses:

  • Anything clouding title or limiting your right to transfer.
  • Well, wastewater, septic and utility hookup trouble.

Section 70-20-502 sets the timing: the buyer gets it ahead of the contract or alongside it. Hand it over later and section 70-20-504 lets the buyer rescind within three days, if that right was not waived. Whichever you lean toward, ask for the expected timeline from signed contract to closing and have it written down. Ask who pays which closing costs too.

Selling with taxes or a loan owed

Money paperwork comes first on any route. Order a payoff statement from your lender, and list liens, back taxes and HOA dues before signing a contract. Tax you owe is settled from the proceeds when the sale closes, and the title company asks the Treasurer for the number.

Pull together the following before you talk to a buyer or agent:

  • Your latest property tax bill and any payment-plan paperwork.
  • The loan payoff statement.
  • Install dates for the roof and furnace.
  • Permits for additions, plus the short-term rental permit if you have one.
  • Notes on the well, septic or road access if the lot is rural.

From contract to closing

After you accept an offer, the title company opens the file. It checks the payoff on your loan, looks for liens, and asks the Treasurer for the tax balance. You sign the disclosure if you have not already, and the buyer either inspects or skips it, depending on the contract. At closing, your lender is paid first, any tax owed is paid next, and what is left is yours. With a cash buyer the loan-approval wait disappears, so the closing date depends mostly on how fast the title work is done. Sellers who answer the title company's requests quickly usually close sooner.

Situations Kalispell sellers run into

When are Flathead County property taxes due?

The first half is due November 30 and the second half is due May 31. Unpaid amounts become delinquent on December 1 and June 1.

Can I pay my Kalispell property tax in monthly installments?

If it is your primary residence, you can ask the Flathead County Treasurer for seven monthly payments from November 30 to May 31. The request is due September 30 of the taxing year.

Do I need a permit to rent my Kalispell house short term?

Most zoned parts of Flathead County require an administrative conditional use permit. Inside the city, check the municipal code or call the city's Development Services Department.

Do I have to disclose problems with my house in Montana?

Yes. Put in writing any adverse material facts you actually know, and deliver it before or with the contract. Some transfers, including court-ordered ones, are exempt.

Can a cash buyer close without an inspection or a loan?

With cash there is no lender, so no loan approval or bank appraisal. Whether the buyer inspects is something the two of you settle in the contract.
